feed.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Anti-Fee-Sniping with LockTime

entry.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Anti-Fee-Sniping with LockTime
entry.summary: The topic of Anti-Fee-Sniping with nLockTime and its associated behaviors in Bitcoin transactions has been a subject of recent discussion. Since its integration, nLockTime has been implemented in Bitcoin Core since 2014 and later in Electrum by 2017, setting a precedent for transaction management in blockchain technology. The proposed BIP (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal) assumes this nLockTime feature as foundational and introduces the use of nSequence for certain taproot spends. Notably, the explicit rules for nLockTime have never been formally documented in a BIP until now. The current draft of the BIP can be found [here](https://github.com/nervana21/bips/blob/anti-fee-snipe/bip-anti-fee-sniping-with-locktime.md), detailing its alignment with Bitcoin Core’s existing functions such as DiscourageFeeSniping and IsCurrentForAntiFeeSniping. According to the proposal, nLockTime is set to the current blockchain tip height, and occasionally, a randomly chosen smaller number is used, enhancing privacy but also presenting potential risks for identifying transaction patterns. Several pertinent issues and observations have been raised concerning the proposed BIP and the overall strategy of Anti-Fee-Sniping. For instance, it was pointed out that BIP125 signaling, which was previously required for a transaction to be deemed replaceable under Bitcoin Core's default mempool policy, is no longer necessary in recent software versions. This change suggests an evolving landscape regarding transaction replacement policies. Additionally, while the technique of back-dating transactions by 10% as a privacy measure does offer some anonymity, it inadvertently creates a risk of these transactions being marked or fingerprinted, particularly when fee-bumping is involved without prior back-dating. This issue is highlighted in discussions on GitHub ([issue #26526](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26526)) and points to the complexity of implementing privacy features without unintended consequences. Moreover, documentation and awareness of edge cases within the BIP could help prevent future misimplementations or misunderstandings. Past instances where wallets attempted to implement Anti-Fee-Sniping unsuccessfully resulted in distinct transaction fingerprints that led to reduced usage of those wallets over time. Current data indicates that only about 5% of transactions employ a height-based time-lock, suggesting a relatively small group of users utilizing this feature, which might not significantly impact overall transaction anonymity if not widely adopted ([transactions with height-based locktime](https://mainnet.observer/charts/transactions-height-based-locktime/)). In conclusion, while the integration of Anti-Fee-Sniping and nLockTime into Bitcoin’s protocol offers strategic advantages for user privacy and transaction security, it also introduces complexities and potential vulnerabilities that need careful consideration. Addressing these concerns through comprehensive documentation and community feedback is crucial for the ongoing development and refinement of Bitcoin’s transaction policies.
